
Convert `Rc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Rc<Any>`. `Rc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Rc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `as_any`

```rust
fn as_any(&self) -> &(dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust
fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut (dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

#### `into_any_rc`

#### `as_any`

```rust

```

#### `as_any_mut`


Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

Converts `self` into a [`Right`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Right) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) otherwise. [Read more](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/into_either/trait.IntoEither.html#method.into_either_with)

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom`

Simple 2D geometric primitives on top of euclid.

This crate is reexported in [lyon](https://docs.rs/lyon/).

## Overview.

This crate implements some of the maths to work with:

- lines and line segments,
- quadratic and cubic bézier curves,
- elliptic arcs,
- triangles.

## Flattening

Flattening is the action of approximating a curve with a succession of line segments.

→

The tolerance threshold taken as input by the flattening algorithms corresponds to the maximum distance between the curve and its linear approximation. The smaller the tolerance is, the more precise the approximation and the more segments are generated. This value is typically chosen in function of the zoom level.

The figure above shows a close up on a curve (the dotted line) and its linear approximation (the black segments). The tolerance threshold is represented by the light green area and the orange arrow.

## Modules

- [`arc`](arc/index.md) — Elliptic arc related maths and tools.
- [`arrayvec`](arrayvec/index.md) — **arrayvec** provides the types [`ArrayVec`](arrayvec/struct.ArrayVec.md) and [`ArrayString`](arrayvec/struct.ArrayString.md): array-backed vector and string types, which store their contents inline.
- [`cubic_bezier`](cubic_bezier/index.md)
- [`euclid`](euclid/index.md) — A collection of strongly typed math tools for computer graphics with an inclination towards 2d graphics and layout.
- [`quadratic_bezier`](quadratic_bezier/index.md)
- [`traits`](traits/index.md)
- [`utils`](utils/index.md)

## Structs

- [`Angle`](struct.Angle.md) — An angle in radians
- [`Arc`](struct.Arc.md) — An elliptic arc curve segment.
- [`ArcFlags`](struct.ArcFlags.md) — Flag parameters for arcs as described by the SVG specification.
- [`CubicBezierSegment`](struct.CubicBezierSegment.md) — A 2d curve segment defined by four points: the beginning of the segment, two control points and the end of the segment.
- [`Line`](struct.Line.md) — An infinite line defined by a point and a vector.
- [`LineEquation`](struct.LineEquation.md) — A line defined by the equation `a * x + b * y + c = 0; a * a + b * b = 1`.
- [`LineSegment`](struct.LineSegment.md) — A linear segment.
- [`QuadraticBezierSegment`](struct.QuadraticBezierSegment.md) — A 2d curve segment defined by three points: the beginning of the segment, a control point and the end of the segment.
- [`SvgArc`](struct.SvgArc.md) — An elliptic arc curve segment using the SVG’s end-point notation.
- [`Triangle`](struct.Triangle.md) — A 2D triangle defined by three points `a`, `b` and `c`.

## Traits

- [`Scalar`](trait.Scalar.md)
- [`Segment`](trait.Segment.md) — Common APIs to segment types.

## Functions

- [`point`](fn.point.md) — Shorthand for `Point::new(x, y)`.
- [`size`](fn.size.md) — Shorthand for `Size::new(x, y)`.
- [`vector`](fn.vector.md) — Shorthand for `Vector::new(x, y)`.

## Type Aliases

- [`Box2D`](type.Box2D.md)
- [`Point`](type.Point.md)
- [`Rotation`](type.Rotation.md) — Alias for `euclid::default::Rotation2D`
- [`Scale`](type.Scale.md)
- [`Size`](type.Size.md)
- [`Transform`](type.Transform.md) — Alias for `euclid::default::Transform2D`
- [`Translation`](type.Translation.md) — Alias for `euclid::default::Translation2D`
- [`Vector`](type.Vector.md)

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::Arc`

```rust
pub struct Arc<S> {
    pub center: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub radii: Vector2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub start_angle: Angle<S>,
    pub sweep_angle: Angle<S>,
    pub x_rotation: Angle<S>,
}
```

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::CubicBezierSegment`

```rust
pub struct CubicBezierSegment<S> {
    pub from: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub ctrl1: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub ctrl2: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub to: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
}
```

A 2d curve segment defined by four points: the beginning of the segment, two control points and the end of the segment.

The curve is defined by equation:² `∀ t ∈ [0..1], P(t) = (1 - t)³ * from + 3 * (1 - t)² * t * ctrl1 + 3 * t² * (1 - t) * ctrl2 + t³ * to`

## Fields

### `from: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>`

### `ctrl1: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>`

### `ctrl2: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>`

### `to: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>`

Approximate the curve with a single quadratic bézier segment.

This is terrible as a general approximation but works if the cubic curve does not have inflection points and is “flat” enough. Typically usable after subdividing the curve a few times.

#### `to_quadratic_error`

#### `is_quadratic`

```rust
pub fn is_quadratic(&self, tolerance: S) -> bool
```

Returns true if the curve can be safely approximated with a single quadratic bézier segment given the provided tolerance threshold.

Equivalent to comparing `to_quadratic_error` with the tolerance threshold, avoiding the cost of two square roots.

#### `num_quadratics`

```rust
pub fn num_quadratics(&self, tolerance: S) -> u32
```

Computes the number of quadratic bézier segments required to approximate this cubic curve given a tolerance threshold.

Derived by Raph Levien from section 10.6 of Sedeberg’s CAGD notes [https://scholarsarchive.byu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=facpub#section.10.6](https://scholarsarchive.byu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=facpub#section.10.6) and the error metric from the caffein owl blog post [http://caffeineowl.com/graphics/2d/vectorial/cubic2quad01.html](http://caffeineowl.com/graphics/2d/vectorial/cubic2quad01.html)

#### `cubic_intersections_t`

```rust
pub fn cubic_intersections_t( &self, curve: &CubicBezierSegment<S>, ) -> ArrayVec<(S, S), 9>
```

Computes the intersections (if any) between this segment and another one.

The result is provided in the form of the `t` parameters of each point along the curves. To get the intersection points, sample the curves at the corresponding values.

Returns endpoint intersections where an endpoint intersects the interior of the other curve, but not endpoint/endpoint intersections.

Returns no intersections if either curve is a point.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::LineEquation`

```rust
pub struct LineEquation<S> { /* private fields */ }
```

A line defined by the equation `a * x + b * y + c = 0; a * a + b * b = 1`.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::QuadraticBezierSegment`

```rust
pub struct QuadraticBezierSegment<S> {
    pub from: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub ctrl: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub to: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
}
```

A 2d curve segment defined by three points: the beginning of the segment, a control point and the end of the segment.

The curve is defined by equation: `∀ t ∈ [0..1], P(t) = (1 - t)² * from + 2 * (1 - t) * t * ctrl + t² * to`

```rust
pub fn square_distance_to_point(&self, pos: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>) -> S
```

Returns the shortest squared distance between this segment and a point.

May be useful to avoid the cost of a square root when comparing against a distance that can be squared instead.

#### `drag`

```rust
pub fn drag( &self, t: S, new_position: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>, ) -> QuadraticBezierSegment<S>
```

#### `length`

```rust
pub fn length(&self) -> S
```

Computes the length of this segment.

Implements Raph Levien’s analytical approach described in https://raphlinus.github.io/curves/2018/12/28/bezier-arclength.html

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::SvgArc`

```rust
pub struct SvgArc<S> {
    pub from: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub to: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub radii: Vector2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub x_rotation: Angle<S>,
    pub flags: ArcFlags,
}
```

An elliptic arc curve segment using the SVG’s end-point notation.

## Fields

### `from: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>`

### `to: Point2D<S, UnknownUnit>`

### `radii: Vector2D<S, UnknownUnit>`

### `x_rotation: Angle<S>`

### `flags: ArcFlags`

## Methods

### `impl<S> SvgArc<S> where S: Scalar,`

#### `to_arc`

```rust
pub fn to_arc(&self) -> Arc<S>
```

Converts this arc from endpoints to center notation.

#### `is_straight_line`

```rust
pub fn is_straight_line(&self) -> bool
```

Per SVG spec, this arc should be rendered as a line_to segment.

Do not convert an `SvgArc` into an `arc` if this returns true.

#### `for_each_quadratic_bezier`

```rust
pub fn for_each_quadratic_bezier<F>(&self, cb: &mut F) where F: FnMut(&QuadraticBezierSegment<S>),
```

Approximates the arc with a sequence of quadratic bézier segments.

#### `for_each_quadratic_bezier_with_t`

```rust
pub fn for_each_quadratic_bezier_with_t<F>(&self, cb: &mut F) where F: FnMut(&QuadraticBezierSegment<S>, Range<S>),
```

Approximates the arc with a sequence of quadratic bézier segments.

#### `for_each_cubic_bezier`

```rust

```

#### `for_each_flattened`

```rust
pub fn for_each_flattened<F>(&self, tolerance: S, cb: &mut F) where F: FnMut(&LineSegment<S>),
```

Approximates the curve with sequence of line segments.

The `tolerance` parameter defines the maximum distance between the curve and its approximation.

#### `for_each_flattened_with_t`

```rust
pub fn for_each_flattened_with_t<F>(&self, tolerance: S, cb: &mut F) where F: FnMut(&LineSegment<S>, Range<S>),
```

Approximates the curve with sequence of line segments.

The `tolerance` parameter defines the maximum distance between the curve and its approximation.

The end of the t parameter range at the final segment is guaranteed to be equal to `1.0`.


Approximates the curve with sequence of line segments.

The `tolerance` parameter defines the maximum distance between the curve and its approximation.

The parameter `t` at the final segment is guaranteed to be equal to `1.0`.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::iterator`

Tools to iterate over paths.

## Lyon path iterators

### Overview

This module provides a collection of traits to extend the `Iterator` trait when iterating over paths.

### Examples

```rust
use lyon_path::iterator::*;
use lyon_path::math::{point, vector};
use lyon_path::{Path, PathEvent};

// Start with a path.
let mut builder = Path::builder();
builder.begin(point(0.0, 0.0));
builder.line_to(point(10.0, 0.0));
builder.cubic_bezier_to(point(10.0, 10.0), point(0.0, 10.0), point(0.0, 5.0));
builder.end(true);
let path = builder.build();

// A simple std::iter::Iterator<PathEvent>,
let simple_iter = path.iter();

// Make it an iterator over simpler primitives flattened events,
// which do not contain any curve. To do so we approximate each curve
// linear segments according to a tolerance threshold which controls
// the tradeoff between fidelity of the approximation and amount of
// generated events. Let's use a tolerance threshold of 0.01.
// The beauty of this approach is that the flattening happens lazily
// while iterating without allocating memory for the path.
let flattened_iter = path.iter().flattened(0.01);

for evt in flattened_iter {
    match evt {
        PathEvent::Begin { at } => { println!(" - move to {:?}", at); }
        PathEvent::Line { from, to } => { println!(" - line {:?} -> {:?}", from, to); }
        PathEvent::End { last, first, close } => {
            if close {
                println!(" - close {:?} -> {:?}", last, first);
            } else {
                println!(" - end");
            }
        }
        _ => { panic!() }
    }
}
```

Chaining the provided iterators allow performing some path manipulations lazily without allocating actual path objects to hold the result of the transformations.

```rust
extern crate lyon_path;
use lyon_path::iterator::*;
use lyon_path::math::{point, Angle, Rotation};
use lyon_path::Path;

fn main() {
    // In practice it is more common to iterate over Path objects than vectors
    // of SVG commands (the former can be constructed from the latter).
    let mut builder = Path::builder();
    builder.begin(point(1.0, 1.0));
    builder.line_to(point(2.0, 1.0));
    builder.quadratic_bezier_to(point(2.0, 2.0), point(1.0, 2.0));
    builder.cubic_bezier_to(point(0.0, 2.0), point(0.0, 0.0), point(1.0, 0.0));
    builder.end(true);
    let path = builder.build();

    let transform = Rotation::new(Angle::radians(1.0));

    for evt in path.iter().transformed(&transform).flattened(0.1) {
        // ...
    }
}
```

## Structs

- [`Flattened`](struct.Flattened.md) — An iterator that consumes `Event` iterator and yields flattened path events (with no curves).
- [`FromPolyline`](struct.FromPolyline.md) — An iterator that consumes an iterator of `Point`s and produces `Event`s.
- [`NoAttributes`](struct.NoAttributes.md)
- [`Transformed`](struct.Transformed.md) — Applies a 2D transform to a path iterator and yields the resulting path iterator.

## Traits

- [`PathIterator`](trait.PathIterator.md) — An extension trait for `PathEvent` iterators.

#### `into_any_rc`

```rust

```

#### `as_any`

```rust

```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust

```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::iterator::FromPolyline`

```rust
pub struct FromPolyline<Iter> { /* private fields */ }
```

An iterator that consumes an iterator of `Point`s and produces `Event`s.

## Example

```rust
let points = [
    point(1.0, 1.0),
    point(2.0, 1.0),
    point(1.0, 2.0)
];
let iter = FromPolyline::closed(points.iter().cloned());
```

#### `into_any_rc`

```rust

```

#### `as_any`

```rust

```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust

```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

#### `into_any`

Convert `Box<dyn Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Box<dyn Any>`. `Box<dyn Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Box<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `into_any_rc`

```rust

```

Convert `Rc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Rc<Any>`. `Rc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Rc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `as_any`

```rust
fn as_any(&self) -> &(dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust
fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut (dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

That is, this conversion is whatever the implementation of `From<T> for U` chooses to do.

Converts `self` into a [`Right`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Right) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) otherwise. [Read more](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/into_either/trait.IntoEither.html#method.into_either)

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::iterator::PathIterator`

```rust
pub trait PathIterator: Sized + Iterator<Item = Event<Point2D<f32, UnknownUnit>, Point2D<f32, UnknownUnit>>> {
    // Provided methods
    fn flattened(self, tolerance: f32) -> Flattened<Self> ⓘ { ... }
    fn transformed<T>(self, mat: &T) -> Transformed<'_, Self, T> ⓘ
       where T: Transformation<f32> { ... }
}
```

An extension trait for `PathEvent` iterators.

## Provided Methods

### `flattened`


Returns an iterator that turns curves into line segments.

### `transformed`

f32 version of the lyon_geom types used everywhere. Most other lyon crates reexport them.

### `impl<T> Downcast for T where T: Any,`

#### `into_any`

```rust
fn into_any(self: Box<T>) -> Box<dyn Any>
```

Convert `Box<dyn Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Box<dyn Any>`. `Box<dyn Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Box<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `into_any_rc`

```rust
fn into_any_rc(self: Rc<T>) -> Rc<dyn Any>
```

Convert `Rc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Rc<Any>`. `Rc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Rc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `as_any`

```rust
fn as_any(&self) -> &(dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust
fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut (dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

### `impl<T> DowncastSync for T where T: Any + Send + Sync,`

#### `into_any_arc`

```rust
fn into_any_arc(self: Arc<T>) -> Arc<dyn Any + Sync + Send>
```

Convert `Arc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Arc<Any>`. `Arc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Arc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

### `impl<T> Downcast for T where T: Any,`

#### `into_any`

#### `into_any_rc`

```rust

```

Convert `Rc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Rc<Any>`. `Rc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Rc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `as_any`

```rust
fn as_any(&self) -> &(dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust
fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut (dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

#### `partial_cmp`

```rust
fn partial_cmp<I>(self, other: I) -> Option<Ordering> where I: IntoIterator, Self::Item: PartialOrd<<I as IntoIterator>::Item>, Self: Sized,
```

[Lexicographically](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html#lexicographical-comparison) compares the [`PartialOrd`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html) elements of this [`Iterator`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) with those of another. The comparison works like short-circuit evaluation, returning a result without comparing the remaining elements. As soon as an order can be determined, the evaluation stops and a result is returned. [Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.partial_cmp)

#### `into_any`

#### `into_any_rc`

```rust

```

Convert `Rc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Rc<Any>`. `Rc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Rc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `as_any`

```rust
fn as_any(&self) -> &(dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust
fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut (dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

```rust
pub struct Flattened<S> { /* private fields */ }
```

Flattening iterator for arcs.

The iterator starts at the first point *after* the origin of the curve and ends at the destination.

#### `as_any`

```rust

```

#### `as_any_mut`


# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::arrayvec`

**arrayvec** provides the types [`ArrayVec`](struct.ArrayVec.md) and [`ArrayString`](struct.ArrayString.md): array-backed vector and string types, which store their contents inline.

The arrayvec package has the following cargo features:

- `std`

  - Optional, enabled by default
  - Use libstd; disable to use `no_std` instead.
- `serde`

  - Optional
  - Enable serialization for ArrayVec and ArrayString using serde 1.x
- `zeroize`

  - Optional
  - Implement `Zeroize` for ArrayVec and ArrayString

### Rust Version

This version of arrayvec requires Rust 1.51 or later.

## Structs

- [`ArrayString`](struct.ArrayString.md) — A string with a fixed capacity.
- [`ArrayVec`](struct.ArrayVec.md) — A vector with a fixed capacity.
- [`CapacityError`](struct.CapacityError.md) — Error value indicating insufficient capacity
- [`Drain`](struct.Drain.md) — A draining iterator for `ArrayVec`.
- [`IntoIter`](struct.IntoIter.md) — By-value iterator for `ArrayVec`.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::arrayvec::ArrayString`

```rust
pub struct ArrayString<const CAP: usize> { /* private fields */ }
```

A string with a fixed capacity.

The `ArrayString` is a string backed by a fixed size array. It keeps track of its length, and is parameterized by `CAP` for the maximum capacity.

`CAP` is of type `usize` but is range limited to `u32::MAX` (or `u16` on 16-bit targets); attempting to create larger arrayvecs with larger capacity will panic.

The string is a contiguous value that you can store directly on the stack if needed.

**Source:** [array_string.rs.html#37](https://docs.rs/arrayvec/0.7/src/arrayvec/array_string.rs.html#37) (lines 37)

## Methods

```rust
pub fn new() -> ArrayString<CAP>
```

Create a new empty `ArrayString`.

Capacity is inferred from the type parameter.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayString;

let mut string = ArrayString::<16>::new();
string.push_str("foo");
assert_eq!(&string[..], "foo");
assert_eq!(string.capacity(), 16);
```

#### `try_push`

```rust
pub fn try_push(&mut self, c: char) -> Result<(), CapacityError<char>>
```

Adds the given char to the end of the string.

Returns `Ok` if the push succeeds.

**Errors** if the backing array is not large enough to fit the additional char.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayString;

let mut string = ArrayString::<2>::new();

string.try_push('a').unwrap();
string.try_push('b').unwrap();
let overflow = string.try_push('c');

assert_eq!(&string[..], "ab");
assert_eq!(overflow.unwrap_err().element(), 'c');
```

```rust
let overflow2 = string.try_push_str("ef");

assert_eq!(overflow1.unwrap_err().element(), "bc");
assert_eq!(overflow2.unwrap_err().element(), "ef");
```

#### `pop`

```rust
pub fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<char>
```

Removes the last character from the string and returns it.

Returns `None` if this `ArrayString` is empty.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayString;

assert_eq!(s.pop(), Some('o'));
assert_eq!(s.pop(), Some('o'));
assert_eq!(s.pop(), Some('f'));

```

#### `truncate`

```rust
pub fn truncate(&mut self, new_len: usize)
```

Shortens this `ArrayString` to the specified length.

If `new_len` is greater than the string’s current length, this has no effect.

***Panics*** if `new_len` does not lie on a `char` boundary.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayString;

let mut string = ArrayString::<6>::from("foobar").unwrap();
string.truncate(3);
assert_eq!(&string[..], "foo");
string.truncate(4);
assert_eq!(&string[..], "foo");
```

#### `remove`

```rust
pub fn remove(&mut self, idx: usize) -> char
```

Removes a `char` from this `ArrayString` at a byte position and returns it.

This is an `O(n)` operation, as it requires copying every element in the array.

***Panics*** if `idx` is larger than or equal to the `ArrayString`’s length, or if it does not lie on a `char` boundary.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayString;

let mut s = ArrayString::<3>::from("foo").unwrap();

assert_eq!(s.remove(0), 'f');
assert_eq!(s.remove(1), 'o');
assert_eq!(s.remove(0), 'o');
```

This method uses *debug assertions* to check the validity of `length` and may use other debug assertions.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::arrayvec::ArrayVec`

```rust
pub struct ArrayVec<T, const CAP: usize> { /* private fields */ }
```

A vector with a fixed capacity.

The `ArrayVec` is a vector backed by a fixed size array. It keeps track of the number of initialized elements. The `ArrayVec<T, CAP>` is parameterized by `T` for the element type and `CAP` for the maximum capacity.

`CAP` is of type `usize` but is range limited to `u32::MAX` (or `u16::MAX` on 16-bit targets); attempting to create larger arrayvecs with larger capacity will panic.

The vector is a contiguous value (storing the elements inline) that you can store directly on the stack if needed.

It offers a simple API but also dereferences to a slice, so that the full slice API is available. The ArrayVec can be converted into a by value iterator.

**Source:** [arrayvec.rs.html#43](https://docs.rs/arrayvec/0.7/src/arrayvec/arrayvec.rs.html#43) (lines 43)

## Methods

### `impl<T, const CAP: usize> ArrayVec<T, CAP>`

#### `new`

```rust
pub fn new() -> ArrayVec<T, CAP>
```

Create a new empty `ArrayVec`.

The maximum capacity is given by the generic parameter `CAP`.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::<_, 16>::new();
array.push(1);
array.push(2);
assert_eq!(&array[..], &[1, 2]);
assert_eq!(array.capacity(), 16);
```

#### `new_const`

```rust
pub const fn new_const() -> ArrayVec<T, CAP>
```

Create a new empty `ArrayVec` (const fn).

The maximum capacity is given by the generic parameter `CAP`.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

static ARRAY: ArrayVec<u8, 1024> = ArrayVec::new_const();
```

#### `len`

```rust
pub const fn len(&self) -> usize
```

Return the number of elements in the `ArrayVec`.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::from([1, 2, 3]);
array.pop();
assert_eq!(array.len(), 2);
```

#### `is_empty`

```rust

```

Returns whether the `ArrayVec` is empty.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

array.pop();
assert_eq!(array.is_empty(), true);
```

#### `capacity`

```rust
pub const fn capacity(&self) -> usize
```

Return the capacity of the `ArrayVec`.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

assert_eq!(array.capacity(), 3);
```

#### `is_full`

```rust
pub const fn is_full(&self) -> bool
```

Return true if the `ArrayVec` is completely filled to its capacity, false otherwise.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::<_, 1>::new();
assert!(!array.is_full());
array.push(1);
assert!(array.is_full());
```

#### `remaining_capacity`


```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::from([1, 2, 3]);
array.pop();
assert_eq!(array.remaining_capacity(), 1);
```

#### `push`

```rust
pub fn push(&mut self, element: T)
```

Push `element` to the end of the vector.

***Panics*** if the vector is already full.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::<_, 2>::new();

array.push(1);
array.push(2);

assert_eq!(&array[..], &[1, 2]);
```

#### `try_push`

```rust
pub fn try_push(&mut self, element: T) -> Result<(), CapacityError<T>>
```

Push `element` to the end of the vector.

Return `Ok` if the push succeeds, or return an error if the vector is already full.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::<_, 2>::new();

let push1 = array.try_push(1);
let push2 = array.try_push(2);

assert!(push1.is_ok());
assert!(push2.is_ok());

assert_eq!(&array[..], &[1, 2]);

let overflow = array.try_push(3);

assert!(overflow.is_err());
```

#### `push_unchecked`

```rust
pub unsafe fn push_unchecked(&mut self, element: T)
```

Push `element` to the end of the vector without checking the capacity.

It is up to the caller to ensure the capacity of the vector is sufficiently large.

This method uses *debug assertions* to check that the arrayvec is not full.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::<_, 2>::new();

if array.len() + 2 <= array.capacity() {
    unsafe {
        array.push_unchecked(1);
        array.push_unchecked(2);
    }
}

assert_eq!(&array[..], &[1, 2]);
```

#### `truncate`

```rust
pub fn truncate(&mut self, new_len: usize)
```

Shortens the vector, keeping the first `len` elements and dropping the rest.

If `len` is greater than the vector’s current length this has no effect.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
array.truncate(3);
assert_eq!(&array[..], &[1, 2, 3]);
array.truncate(4);
assert_eq!(&array[..], &[1, 2, 3]);
```

#### `clear`

```rust
pub fn clear(&mut self)
```

Remove all elements in the vector.

#### `insert`

```rust
pub fn insert(&mut self, index: usize, element: T)
```

Insert `element` at position `index`.

Shift up all elements after `index`.

It is an error if the index is greater than the length or if the arrayvec is full.

***Panics*** if the array is full or the `index` is out of bounds. See `try_insert` for fallible version.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::<_, 2>::new();

array.insert(0, "x");
array.insert(0, "y");
assert_eq!(&array[..], &["y", "x"]);
```

#### `try_insert`

```rust
pub fn try_insert( &mut self, index: usize, element: T, ) -> Result<(), CapacityError<T>>
```

Insert `element` at position `index`.

Shift up all elements after `index`; the `index` must be less than or equal to the length.

Returns an error if vector is already at full capacity.

***Panics*** `index` is out of bounds.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::<_, 2>::new();

assert!(array.try_insert(0, "x").is_ok());
assert!(array.try_insert(0, "y").is_ok());
assert!(array.try_insert(0, "z").is_err());
assert_eq!(&array[..], &["y", "x"]);
```

#### `pop`

```rust
pub fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<T>
```

Remove the last element in the vector and return it.

Return `Some(` *element* `)` if the vector is non-empty, else `None`.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::<_, 2>::new();

array.push(1);

assert_eq!(array.pop(), Some(1));
assert_eq!(array.pop(), None);
```

#### `swap_remove`

```rust
pub fn swap_remove(&mut self, index: usize) -> T
```

Remove the element at `index` and swap the last element into its place.

This operation is O(1).

Return the *element* if the index is in bounds, else panic.

***Panics*** if the `index` is out of bounds.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::from([1, 2, 3]);

assert_eq!(array.swap_remove(0), 1);
assert_eq!(&array[..], &[3, 2]);

assert_eq!(array.swap_remove(1), 2);
assert_eq!(&array[..], &[3]);
```

#### `swap_pop`

```rust
pub fn swap_pop(&mut self, index: usize) -> Option<T>
```

Remove the element at `index` and swap the last element into its place.

This is a checked version of `.swap_remove`.
This operation is O(1).

Return `Some(` *element* `)` if the index is in bounds, else `None`.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::from([1, 2, 3]);

assert_eq!(array.swap_pop(0), Some(1));
assert_eq!(&array[..], &[3, 2]);

assert_eq!(array.swap_pop(10), None);
```

#### `remove`

```rust
pub fn remove(&mut self, index: usize) -> T
```

Remove the element at `index` and shift down the following elements.

The `index` must be strictly less than the length of the vector.

***Panics*** if the `index` is out of bounds.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::from([1, 2, 3]);

let removed_elt = array.remove(0);
assert_eq!(removed_elt, 1);
assert_eq!(&array[..], &[2, 3]);
```

#### `pop_at`

```rust
pub fn pop_at(&mut self, index: usize) -> Option<T>
```

Remove the element at `index` and shift down the following elements.

This is a checked version of `.remove(index)`. Returns `None` if there is no element at `index`. Otherwise, return the element inside `Some`.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::from([1, 2, 3]);

assert!(array.pop_at(0).is_some());
assert_eq!(&array[..], &[2, 3]);

assert!(array.pop_at(2).is_none());
assert!(array.pop_at(10).is_none());
```

#### `retain`

```rust
pub fn retain<F>(&mut self, f: F) where F: FnMut(&mut T) -> bool,
```

Retains only the elements specified by the predicate.

In other words, remove all elements `e` such that `f(&mut e)` returns false. This method operates in place and preserves the order of the retained elements.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut array = ArrayVec::from([1, 2, 3, 4]);
array.retain(|x| *x & 1 != 0 );
assert_eq!(&array[..], &[1, 3]);
```

#### `spare_capacity_mut`

```rust
pub fn spare_capacity_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [MaybeUninit<T>]
```

Returns the remaining spare capacity of the vector as a slice of `MaybeUninit<T>`.

The returned slice can be used to fill the vector with data (e.g. by reading from a file) before marking the data as initialized using the [`set_len`](struct.ArrayVec.md) method.

###### Examples

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

// Allocate vector big enough for 10 elements.
let mut v: ArrayVec<i32, 10> = ArrayVec::new();

// Fill in the first 3 elements.
let uninit = v.spare_capacity_mut();
uninit[0].write(0);
uninit[1].write(1);
uninit[2].write(2);

// Mark the first 3 elements of the vector as being initialized.
unsafe {
    v.set_len(3);
}

assert_eq!(&v[..], &[0, 1, 2]);
```

#### `set_len`

```rust
pub unsafe fn set_len(&mut self, length: usize)
```

Set the vector’s length without dropping or moving out elements

This method is `unsafe` because it changes the notion of the number of “valid” elements in the vector. Use with care.

This method uses *debug assertions* to check that `length` is not greater than the capacity.

#### `try_extend_from_slice`

```rust
pub fn try_extend_from_slice( &mut self, other: &[T], ) -> Result<(), CapacityError> where T: Copy,
```

Copy all elements from the slice and append to the `ArrayVec`.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut vec: ArrayVec<usize, 10> = ArrayVec::new();
vec.push(1);
vec.try_extend_from_slice(&[2, 3]).unwrap();
assert_eq!(&vec[..], &[1, 2, 3]);
```

###### Errors

This method will return an error if the capacity left (see `remaining_capacity`) is smaller then the length of the provided slice.

#### `drain`

```rust
pub fn drain<R>(&mut self, range: R) -> Drain<'_, T, CAP> ⓘ where R: RangeBounds<usize>,
```

Create a draining iterator that removes the specified range in the vector and yields the removed items from start to end. The element range is removed even if the iterator is not consumed until the end.

Note: It is unspecified how many elements are removed from the vector, if the `Drain` value is leaked.

**Panics** if the starting point is greater than the end point or if the end point is greater than the length of the vector.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut v1 = ArrayVec::from([1, 2, 3]);
let v2: ArrayVec<_, 3> = v1.drain(0..2).collect();
assert_eq!(&v1[..], &[3]);
assert_eq!(&v2[..], &[1, 2]);
```

#### `into_inner`

```rust
pub fn into_inner(self) -> Result<[T; CAP], ArrayVec<T, CAP>>
```

Return the inner fixed size array, if it is full to its capacity.

Return an `Ok` value with the array if length equals capacity, return an `Err` with self otherwise.

#### `into_inner_unchecked`

```rust
pub unsafe fn into_inner_unchecked(self) -> [T; CAP]
```

Return the inner fixed size array.

Safety: This operation is safe if and only if length equals capacity.

#### `take`

```rust
pub fn take(&mut self) -> ArrayVec<T, CAP>
```

Returns the ArrayVec, replacing the original with a new empty ArrayVec.

```rust
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

let mut v = ArrayVec::from([0, 1, 2, 3]);
assert_eq!([0, 1, 2, 3], v.take().into_inner().unwrap());
assert!(v.is_empty());
```

#### `as_slice`

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust
fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut (dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

### `impl<T> DowncastSync for T where T: Any + Send + Sync,`

#### `into_any_arc`

```rust
fn into_any_arc(self: Arc<T>) -> Arc<dyn Any + Sync + Send>
```

Convert `Arc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Arc<Any>`. `Arc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Arc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

### `impl<T> IntoEither for T`

Converts `self` into a [`Left`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Left) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) if `into_left` is `true`. Converts `self` into a [`Right`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Right) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) otherwise. [Read more](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/into_either/trait.IntoEither.html#method.into_either)

#### `into_either_with`

```rust

```

Converts `self` into a [`Left`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Left) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) if `into_left(&self)` returns `true`. Converts `self` into a [`Right`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Right) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) otherwise. [Read more](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/into_either/trait.IntoEither.html#method.into_either_with)

### `impl<T> Downcast for T where T: Any,`

#### `into_any`

```rust

```

Convert `Box<dyn Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Box<dyn Any>`. `Box<dyn Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Box<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `into_any_rc`

```rust
fn into_any_rc(self: Rc<T>) -> Rc<dyn Any>
```

Convert `Rc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Rc<Any>`. `Rc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Rc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `as_any`

```rust
fn as_any(&self) -> &(dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust
fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut (dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

### `impl<T> Downcast for T where T: Any,`

#### `into_any`

```rust

```

Convert `Box<dyn Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Box<dyn Any>`. `Box<dyn Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Box<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `into_any_rc`

```rust

```

Convert `Rc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Rc<Any>`. `Rc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Rc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `as_any`

```rust
fn as_any(&self) -> &(dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust
fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut (dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

### `impl<T> IntoEither for T`

#### `into_either`

```rust
fn into_either(self, into_left: bool) -> Either<Self, Self>
```

Converts `self` into a [`Left`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Left) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) if `into_left` is `true`. Converts `self` into a [`Right`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Right) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) otherwise. [Read more](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/into_either/trait.IntoEither.html#method.into_either)

#### `into_either_with`

```rust

```

Converts `self` into a [`Left`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Left) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) if `into_left(&self)` returns `true`. Converts `self` into a [`Right`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html#variant.Right) variant of [`Either<Self, Self>`](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/enum.Either.html) otherwise. [Read more](https://docs.rs/either/1/either/into_either/trait.IntoEither.html#method.into_either_with)

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::cubic_bezier::CubicBezierPolynomial`

```rust
pub struct CubicBezierPolynomial<S> {
    pub a0: Vector2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub a1: Vector2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub a2: Vector2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
    pub a3: Vector2D<S, UnknownUnit>,
}
```

The polynomial form of a cubic bézier segment.

The `sample` implementation uses Horner’s method and tends to be faster than `CubicBezierSegment::sample`.

#### `as_any`

```rust

```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust

```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::euclid`

A collection of strongly typed math tools for computer graphics with an inclination towards 2d graphics and layout.

All types are generic over the scalar type of their component (`f32`, `i32`, etc.), and tagged with a generic Unit parameter which is useful to prevent mixing values from different spaces. For example it should not be legal to translate a screen-space position by a world-space vector and this can be expressed using the generic Unit parameter.

This unit system is not mandatory and all structures have an alias with the default unit: `UnknownUnit`. for example `default::Point2D<T>` is equivalent to `Point2D<T, UnknownUnit>`. Client code typically creates a set of aliases for each type and doesn’t need to deal with the specifics of typed units further. For example:

```rust
use euclid::*;
pub struct ScreenSpace;
pub type ScreenPoint = Point2D<f32, ScreenSpace>;
pub type ScreenSize = Size2D<f32, ScreenSpace>;
pub struct WorldSpace;
pub type WorldPoint = Point3D<f32, WorldSpace>;
pub type ProjectionMatrix = Transform3D<f32, WorldSpace, ScreenSpace>;
// etc...
```

All euclid types are marked `#[repr(C)]` in order to facilitate exposing them to foreign function interfaces (provided the underlying scalar type is also `repr(C)`).

## Modules

- [`approxeq`](approxeq/index.md) *(std or libm)*
- [`approxord`](approxord/index.md) — Utilities for testing approximate ordering - especially true for floating point types, where NaN’s cannot be ordered.
- [`default`](default/index.md) — A set of aliases for all types, tagged with the default unknown unit.
- [`num`](num/index.md) — A one-dimensional length, tagged with its units.

## Structs

- [`Angle`](struct.Angle.md) — An angle in radians
- [`BoolVector2D`](struct.BoolVector2D.md) — A 2d vector of booleans, useful for component-wise logic operations.
- [`BoolVector3D`](struct.BoolVector3D.md) — A 3d vector of booleans, useful for component-wise logic operations.
- [`Box2D`](struct.Box2D.md) — A 2d axis aligned rectangle represented by its minimum and maximum coordinates.
- [`Box3D`](struct.Box3D.md) — An axis aligned 3D box represented by its minimum and maximum coordinates.
- [`HomogeneousVector`](struct.HomogeneousVector.md) — Homogeneous vector in 3D space.
- [`Length`](struct.Length.md) — A one-dimensional distance, with value represented by `T` and unit of measurement `Unit`.
- [`Point2D`](struct.Point2D.md) — A 2d Point tagged with a unit.
- [`Point3D`](struct.Point3D.md) — A 3d Point tagged with a unit.
- [`Rect`](struct.Rect.md) — A 2d Rectangle optionally tagged with a unit.
- [`RigidTransform3D`](struct.RigidTransform3D.md) — A rigid transformation. All lengths are preserved under such a transformation.
- [`Rotation2D`](struct.Rotation2D.md) — A transform that can represent rotations in 2d, represented as an angle in radians.
- [`Rotation3D`](struct.Rotation3D.md) — A transform that can represent rotations in 3d, represented as a quaternion.
- [`Scale`](struct.Scale.md) — A scaling factor between two different units of measurement.
- [`ScaleOffset2D`](struct.ScaleOffset2D.md)
- [`SideOffsets2D`](struct.SideOffsets2D.md) — A group of 2D side offsets, which correspond to top/right/bottom/left for borders, padding, and margins in CSS, optionally tagged with a unit.
- [`Size2D`](struct.Size2D.md) — A 2d size tagged with a unit.
- [`Size3D`](struct.Size3D.md) — A 3d size tagged with a unit.
- [`Transform2D`](struct.Transform2D.md) — A 2d transform represented by a column-major 3 by 3 matrix, compressed down to 3 by 2.
- [`Transform3D`](struct.Transform3D.md) — A 3d transform stored as a column-major 4 by 4 matrix.
- [`Translation2D`](struct.Translation2D.md) — A 2d transformation from a space to another that can only express translations.
- [`Translation3D`](struct.Translation3D.md) — A 3d transformation from a space to another that can only express translations.
- [`UnknownUnit`](struct.UnknownUnit.md) — The default unit.
- [`Vector2D`](struct.Vector2D.md) — A 2d Vector tagged with a unit.
- [`Vector3D`](struct.Vector3D.md) — A 3d Vector tagged with a unit.

## Traits

- [`Trig`](trait.Trig.md) — Trait for basic trigonometry functions, so they can be used on generic numeric types

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::euclid::Box2D`

```rust
#[repr(C)]pub struct Box2D<T, U> {
    pub min: Point2D<T, U>,
    pub max: Point2D<T, U>,
}
```

A 2d axis aligned rectangle represented by its minimum and maximum coordinates.

## Representation

This struct is similar to [`Rect`](struct.Rect.md), but stores rectangle as two endpoints instead of origin point and size. Such representation has several advantages over [`Rect`](struct.Rect.md) representation:

- Several operations are more efficient with `Box2D`, including [`intersection`](struct.Box2D.md), [`union`](struct.Box2D.md), and point-in-rect.
- The representation is less susceptible to overflow. With [`Rect`](struct.Rect.md), computation of second point can overflow for a large range of values of origin and size. However, with `Box2D`, computation of [`size`](struct.Box2D.md) cannot overflow if the coordinates are signed and the resulting size is unsigned.

A known disadvantage of `Box2D` is that translating the rectangle requires translating both points, whereas translating [`Rect`](struct.Rect.md) only requires translating one point.

## Empty box

A box is considered empty (see [`is_empty`](struct.Box2D.md)) if any of the following is true:

- it’s area is empty,
- it’s area is negative (`min.x > max.x` or `min.y > max.y`),
- it contains NaNs.

#### `is_negative`

```rust
pub fn is_negative(&self) -> bool
```

The common interpretation for a negative box is to consider it empty. It can be obtained by calculating the intersection of two boxes that do not intersect.


#### `intersects`

```rust
pub fn intersects(&self, other: &Box2D<T, U>) -> bool
```

Returns `true` if the two boxes intersect.

#### `contains`

```rust
pub fn contains(&self, p: Point2D<T, U>) -> bool
```

Returns `true` if this [`Box2D`](struct.Box2D.md) contains the point `p`.

Points on the top and left edges are inside the box, whereas points on the bottom and right edges are outside the box. See [`Box2D::contains_inclusive`](struct.Box2D.md) for a variant that also includes those latter points.

###### Examples

```rust
use euclid::default::{Box2D, Point2D};

let rect = Box2D::new(Point2D::origin(), Point2D::new(2, 2));

assert!(rect.contains(Point2D::new(1, 1)));

assert!(rect.contains(Point2D::new(0, 1))); // left edge
assert!(rect.contains(Point2D::new(1, 0))); // top edge
assert!(rect.contains(Point2D::origin()));

assert!(!rect.contains(Point2D::new(2, 1))); // right edge
assert!(!rect.contains(Point2D::new(1, 2))); // bottom edge
assert!(!rect.contains(Point2D::new(2, 2)));
```

#### `contains_inclusive`

```rust
pub fn contains_inclusive(&self, p: Point2D<T, U>) -> bool
```

Returns `true` if this box contains the point `p`.

This is like [`Box2D::contains`](struct.Box2D.md), but points on the bottom and right edges are also inside the box.

###### Examples

```rust
use euclid::default::{Box2D, Point2D};

let rect = Box2D::new(Point2D::origin(), Point2D::new(2, 2));

assert!(rect.contains_inclusive(Point2D::new(1, 1)));

assert!(rect.contains_inclusive(Point2D::new(0, 1))); // left edge
assert!(rect.contains_inclusive(Point2D::new(1, 0))); // top edge
assert!(rect.contains_inclusive(Point2D::origin()));

assert!(rect.contains_inclusive(Point2D::new(2, 1))); // right edge
assert!(rect.contains_inclusive(Point2D::new(1, 2))); // bottom edge
assert!(rect.contains_inclusive(Point2D::new(2, 2)));
```

#### `contains_box`

```rust
pub fn contains_box(&self, other: &Box2D<T, U>) -> bool
```

Returns `true` if this box contains the interior of the other box. Always returns `true` if other is empty, and always returns `false` if other is nonempty but this box is empty.

### `impl<T, U> Box2D<T, U> where T: Copy + Zero + PartialOrd,`

#### `from_points`

```rust
pub fn from_points<I>(points: I) -> Box2D<T, U> where I: IntoIterator, <I as IntoIterator>::Item: Borrow<Point2D<T, U>>,
```

Returns the smallest box enclosing all of the provided points.

The top/bottom/left/right-most points are exactly on the box’s edges. Since [`Box2D::contains`](struct.Box2D.md) excludes points that are on the right-most and bottom-most edges, not all points passed to [`Box2D::from_points`](struct.Box2D.md) are contained in the returned [`Box2D`](struct.Box2D.md) when probed with [`Box2D::contains`](struct.Box2D.md), but are when probed with [`Box2D::contains_inclusive`](struct.Box2D.md).

For example:

```rust
use euclid::default::{Point2D, Box2D};

let a = Point2D::origin();
let b = Point2D::new(1, 2);
let rect = Box2D::from_points([a, b]);

assert_eq!(rect.width(), 1);
assert_eq!(rect.height(), 2);

assert!(rect.contains(a));
assert!(!rect.contains(b));
assert!(rect.contains_inclusive(b));
```

In particular, calling [`Box2D::from_points`](struct.Box2D.md) with a single point results in an empty [`Box2D`](struct.Box2D.md):

```rust
use euclid::default::{Point2D, Box2D};

let a = Point2D::new(1, 0);
let rect = Box2D::from_points([a]);

assert!(rect.is_empty());
assert!(!rect.contains(a));
assert!(rect.contains_inclusive(a));
```

The [`Box2D`](struct.Box2D.md) enclosing no points is also empty:

```rust
use euclid::default::{Box2D, Point2D};

let rect = Box2D::from_points(std::iter::empty::<Point2D<i32>>());
assert!(rect.is_empty());
```

#### `cast`

```rust
pub fn cast<NewT>(&self) -> Box2D<NewT, U> where NewT: NumCast,
```

Cast from one numeric representation to another, preserving the units.

When casting from floating point to integer coordinates, the decimals are truncated as one would expect from a simple cast, but this behavior does not always make sense geometrically. Consider using [`round`](struct.Box2D.md), [`round_in`](struct.Box2D.md) or [`round_out`](struct.Box2D.md) before casting.

### `impl<T, U> Box2D<T, U> where T: Round,`

#### `round`

```rust
pub fn round(&self) -> Box2D<T, U>
```

Return a box with edges rounded to integer coordinates, such that the returned box has the same set of pixel centers as the original one. Values equal to 0.5 round up. Suitable for most places where integral device coordinates are needed, but note that any translation should be applied first to avoid pixel rounding errors. Note that this is *not* rounding to nearest integer if the values are negative. They are always rounding as floor(n + 0.5).

### `impl<T, U> Box2D<T, U> where T: Floor + Ceil,`

#### `round_in`

```rust
pub fn round_in(&self) -> Box2D<T, U>
```

Return a box with faces/edges rounded to integer coordinates, such that the original box contains the resulting box.

#### `round_out`

```rust
pub fn round_out(&self) -> Box2D<T, U>
```

Return a box with faces/edges rounded to integer coordinates, such that the original box is contained in the resulting box.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::euclid::Box3D`

```rust
#[repr(C)]pub struct Box3D<T, U> {
    pub min: Point3D<T, U>,
    pub max: Point3D<T, U>,
}
```

An axis aligned 3D box represented by its minimum and maximum coordinates.

### `impl<T, U> Box3D<T, U> where T: PartialOrd,`

#### `is_negative`

```rust
pub fn is_negative(&self) -> bool
```

Returns `true` if the box has a negative volume.

The common interpretation for a negative box is to consider it empty. It can be obtained by calculating the intersection of two boxes that do not intersect.

#### `is_empty`

```rust
pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool
```

```rust

```

#### `contains`

```rust
pub fn contains(&self, other: Point3D<T, U>) -> bool
```

Returns `true` if this [`Box3D`](struct.Box3D.md) contains the point `p`.

Points on the front, left, and top faces are inside the box, whereas points on the back, right, and bottom faces are outside the box. See [`Box3D::contains_inclusive`](struct.Box3D.md) for a variant that also includes those latter points.

###### Examples

```rust
use euclid::default::{Box3D, Point3D};

let cube = Box3D::new(Point3D::origin(), Point3D::new(2, 2, 2));

assert!(cube.contains(Point3D::new(1, 1, 1)));

assert!(cube.contains(Point3D::new(0, 1, 1))); // front face
assert!(cube.contains(Point3D::new(1, 0, 1))); // left face
assert!(cube.contains(Point3D::new(1, 1, 0))); // top face
assert!(cube.contains(Point3D::new(0, 0, 0)));

assert!(!cube.contains(Point3D::new(2, 1, 1))); // back face
assert!(!cube.contains(Point3D::new(1, 2, 1))); // right face
assert!(!cube.contains(Point3D::new(1, 1, 2))); // bottom face
assert!(!cube.contains(Point3D::new(2, 2, 2)));
```

#### `contains_inclusive`

```rust
pub fn contains_inclusive(&self, other: Point3D<T, U>) -> bool
```

Returns `true` if this [`Box3D`](struct.Box3D.md) contains the point `p`.

This is like [`Box3D::contains`](struct.Box3D.md), but points on the back, right, and bottom faces are also inside the box.

###### Examples

```rust
use euclid::default::{Box3D, Point3D};

let cube = Box3D::new(Point3D::origin(), Point3D::new(2, 2, 2));

assert!(cube.contains_inclusive(Point3D::new(1, 1, 1)));

assert!(cube.contains_inclusive(Point3D::new(0, 1, 1))); // front face
assert!(cube.contains_inclusive(Point3D::new(1, 0, 1))); // left face
assert!(cube.contains_inclusive(Point3D::new(1, 1, 0))); // top face
assert!(cube.contains_inclusive(Point3D::new(0, 0, 0))); // front-left-top corner

assert!(cube.contains_inclusive(Point3D::new(2, 1, 1))); // back face
assert!(cube.contains_inclusive(Point3D::new(1, 2, 1))); // right face
assert!(cube.contains_inclusive(Point3D::new(1, 1, 2))); // bottom face
assert!(cube.contains_inclusive(Point3D::new(2, 2, 2))); // back-right-bottom corner
```

#### `contains_box`

```rust
pub fn contains_box(&self, other: &Box3D<T, U>) -> bool
```

Returns `true` if this box3d contains the interior of the other box3d. Always returns `true` if other is empty, and always returns `false` if other is nonempty but this box3d is empty.

### `impl<T, U> Box3D<T, U> where T: Copy + Zero + PartialOrd,`

#### `from_points`

```rust
pub fn from_points<I>(points: I) -> Box3D<T, U> where I: IntoIterator, <I as IntoIterator>::Item: Borrow<Point3D<T, U>>,
```

Returns the smallest box enclosing all of the provided points.

The top/bottom/left/right/front/back-most points are exactly on the box’s edges. Since [`Box3D::contains`](struct.Box3D.md) excludes points that are on the right/bottom/back-most faces, not all points passed to [`Box3D::from_points`](struct.Box3D.md) are contained in the returned [`Box3D`](struct.Box3D.md) when probed with [`Box3D::contains`](struct.Box3D.md), but are when probed with [`Box3D::contains_inclusive`](struct.Box3D.md).

For example:

```rust
use euclid::default::{Point3D, Box3D};

let a = Point3D::origin();
let b = Point3D::new(1, 2, 3);
let box3 = Box3D::from_points([a, b]);

assert_eq!(box3.width(), 1);
assert_eq!(box3.height(), 2);
assert_eq!(box3.depth(), 3);

assert!(box3.contains(a));
assert!(!box3.contains(b));
assert!(box3.contains_inclusive(b));
```

In particular, calling [`Box3D::from_points`](struct.Box3D.md) with a single point results in an empty [`Box3D`](struct.Box3D.md):

```rust
use euclid::default::{Point3D, Box3D};

let a = Point3D::new(1, 0, 1);
let box3 = Box3D::from_points([a]);

assert!(box3.is_empty());
assert!(!box3.contains(a));
assert!(box3.contains_inclusive(a));
```

The [`Box3D`](struct.Box3D.md) enclosing no points is also empty:

```rust
use euclid::default::{Box3D, Point3D};

let box3 = Box3D::from_points(std::iter::empty::<Point3D<i32>>());
assert!(box3.is_empty());
```

### `impl<T, U> Box3D<T, U> where T: NumCast + Copy,`

#### `cast`

```rust
pub fn cast<NewT>(&self) -> Box3D<NewT, U> where NewT: NumCast,
```

Cast from one numeric representation to another, preserving the units.

When casting from floating point to integer coordinates, the decimals are truncated as one would expect from a simple cast, but this behavior does not always make sense geometrically. Consider using [`round`](struct.Box3D.md), [`round_in`](struct.Box3D.md) or [`round_out`](struct.Box3D.md) before casting.

#### `try_cast`

```rust
pub fn try_cast<NewT>(&self) -> Option<Box3D<NewT, U>> where NewT: NumCast,
```

### `impl<T, U> Box3D<T, U> where T: Round,`

#### `round`

```rust
pub fn round(&self) -> Box3D<T, U>
```

Return a box3d with edges rounded to integer coordinates, such that the returned box3d has the same set of pixel centers as the original one. Values equal to 0.5 round up. Suitable for most places where integral device coordinates are needed, but note that any translation should be applied first to avoid pixel rounding errors. Note that this is *not* rounding to nearest integer if the values are negative. They are always rounding as floor(n + 0.5).

### `impl<T, U> Box3D<T, U> where T: Floor + Ceil,`

#### `round_in`

```rust
pub fn round_in(&self) -> Box3D<T, U>
```

Return a box3d with faces/edges rounded to integer coordinates, such that the original box3d contains the resulting box3d.

#### `round_out`

```rust
pub fn round_out(&self) -> Box3D<T, U>
```

Return a box3d with faces/edges rounded to integer coordinates, such that the original box3d is contained in the resulting box3d.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::euclid::Length`

```rust
pub struct Length<T, Unit>(pub T, _);
```

A one-dimensional distance, with value represented by `T` and unit of measurement `Unit`.

`T` can be any numeric type, for example a primitive type like `u64` or `f32`.

`Unit` is not used in the representation of a `Length` value. It is used only at compile time to ensure that a `Length` stored with one unit is converted explicitly before being used in an expression that requires a different unit. It may be a type without values, such as an empty enum.

You can multiply a `Length` by a [`Scale`](struct.Scale.md) to convert it from one unit to another. See the [`Scale`](struct.Scale.md) docs for an example.


Unpack the underlying value from the wrapper.

#### `cast_unit`

```rust
pub fn cast_unit<V>(self) -> Length<T, V>
```

Cast the unit

#### `lerp`

```rust
pub fn lerp(self, other: Length<T, U>, t: T) -> Length<T, U> where T: One + Sub<Output = T> + Mul<Output = T> + Add<Output = T>,
```

Linearly interpolate between this length and another length.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::default::Length;

let from = Length::new(0.0);
let to = Length::new(8.0);

assert_eq!(from.lerp(to, -1.0), Length::new(-8.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  0.0), Length::new( 0.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  0.5), Length::new( 4.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  1.0), Length::new( 8.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  2.0), Length::new(16.0));
```

This behavior is preserved for negative values (unlike the basic cast).

#### `lerp`

```rust
pub fn lerp(self, other: Point2D<T, U>, t: T) -> Point2D<T, U> where T: One + Sub<Output = T> + Mul<Output = T> + Add<Output = T>,
```

Linearly interpolate between this point and another point.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::point2;
use euclid::default::Point2D;

let from: Point2D<_> = point2(0.0, 10.0);
let to:  Point2D<_> = point2(8.0, -4.0);

assert_eq!(from.lerp(to, -1.0), point2(-8.0,  24.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  0.0), point2( 0.0,  10.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  0.5), point2( 4.0,   3.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  1.0), point2( 8.0,  -4.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  2.0), point2(16.0, -18.0));
```

### `impl<T, U> Point2D<T, U> where T: Euclid,`

#### `rem_euclid`

```rust
pub fn rem_euclid(&self, other: &Size2D<T, U>) -> Point2D<T, U>
```

Calculates the least nonnegative remainder of `self (mod other)`.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::point2;
use euclid::default::{Point2D, Size2D};

let p = Point2D::new(7.0, -7.0);
let s = Size2D::new(4.0, -4.0);

assert_eq!(p.rem_euclid(&s), point2(3.0, 1.0));
assert_eq!((-p).rem_euclid(&s), point2(1.0, 3.0));
assert_eq!(p.rem_euclid(&-s), point2(3.0, 1.0));
```

#### `div_euclid`

```rust
pub fn div_euclid(&self, other: &Size2D<T, U>) -> Point2D<T, U>
```

Calculates Euclidean division, the matching method for `rem_euclid`.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::point2;
use euclid::default::{Point2D, Size2D};

let p = Point2D::new(7.0, -7.0);
let s = Size2D::new(4.0, -4.0);

assert_eq!(p.div_euclid(&s), point2(1.0, 2.0));
assert_eq!((-p).div_euclid(&s), point2(-2.0, -1.0));
assert_eq!(p.div_euclid(&-s), point2(-1.0, -2.0));
```

Tag a unitless value with units.

#### `map`

```rust
pub fn map<V, F>(self, f: F) -> Point3D<V, U> where F: FnMut(T) -> V,
```

Apply the function `f` to each component of this point.

###### Example

This may be used to perform unusual arithmetic which is not already offered as methods.

```rust
use euclid::default::Point3D;

let p = Point3D::<u32>::new(5, 11, 15);
assert_eq!(p.map(|coord| coord.saturating_sub(10)), Point3D::new(0, 1, 5));
```

#### `zip`

```rust
pub fn zip<V, F>(self, rhs: Point3D<T, U>, f: F) -> Vector3D<V, U> where F: FnMut(T, T) -> V,
```

Apply the function `f` to each pair of components of this point and `rhs`.

###### Example

This may be used to perform unusual arithmetic which is not already offered as methods.

```rust
use euclid::{default::{Point3D, Vector3D}, point2};

let a: Point3D<u32> = Point3D::new(50, 200, 400);
let b: Point3D<u32> = Point3D::new(100, 100, 150);
assert_eq!(a.zip(b, u32::saturating_sub), Vector3D::new(0, 100, 250));
```

#### `round`

```rust
pub fn round(self) -> Point3D<T, U> where T: Round,
```

Rounds each component to the nearest integer value.

This behavior is preserved for negative values (unlike the basic cast).

```rust
enum Mm {}

assert_eq!(point3::<_, Mm>(-0.1, -0.8, 0.4).round(), point3::<_, Mm>(0.0, -1.0, 0.0))
```

#### `ceil`

```rust
pub fn ceil(self) -> Point3D<T, U> where T: Ceil,
```

Rounds each component to the smallest integer equal or greater than the original value.

This behavior is preserved for negative values (unlike the basic cast).

```rust
enum Mm {}

assert_eq!(point3::<_, Mm>(-0.1, -0.8, 0.4).ceil(), point3::<_, Mm>(0.0, 0.0, 1.0))
```

#### `floor`

```rust
pub fn floor(self) -> Point3D<T, U> where T: Floor,
```

Rounds each component to the biggest integer equal or lower than the original value.

This behavior is preserved for negative values (unlike the basic cast).

```rust
enum Mm {}

assert_eq!(point3::<_, Mm>(-0.1, -0.8, 0.4).floor(), point3::<_, Mm>(-1.0, -1.0, 0.0))
```

#### `lerp`

```rust
pub fn lerp(self, other: Point3D<T, U>, t: T) -> Point3D<T, U> where T: One + Sub<Output = T> + Mul<Output = T> + Add<Output = T>,
```

Linearly interpolate between this point and another point.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::point3;
use euclid::default::Point3D;

let from: Point3D<_> = point3(0.0, 10.0, -1.0);
let to:  Point3D<_> = point3(8.0, -4.0,  0.0);

assert_eq!(from.lerp(to, -1.0), point3(-8.0,  24.0, -2.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  0.0), point3( 0.0,  10.0, -1.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  0.5), point3( 4.0,   3.0, -0.5));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  1.0), point3( 8.0,  -4.0,  0.0));
assert_eq!(from.lerp(to,  2.0), point3(16.0, -18.0,  1.0));
```

### `impl<T, U> Point3D<T, U> where T: NumCast + Copy,`


Cast from one numeric representation to another, preserving the units.

When casting from floating point to integer coordinates, the decimals are truncated as one would expect from a simple cast, but this behavior does not always make sense geometrically. Consider using `round()`, `ceil()` or `floor()` before casting.

### `impl<T, U> Point3D<T, U> where T: Euclid,`

#### `rem_euclid`

```rust
pub fn rem_euclid(&self, other: &Size3D<T, U>) -> Point3D<T, U>
```

Calculates the least nonnegative remainder of `self (mod other)`.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::point3;
use euclid::default::{Point3D, Size3D};

let p = Point3D::new(7.0, -7.0, 0.0);
let s = Size3D::new(4.0, -4.0, 12.0);

assert_eq!(p.rem_euclid(&s), point3(3.0, 1.0, 0.0));
assert_eq!((-p).rem_euclid(&s), point3(1.0, 3.0, 0.0));
assert_eq!(p.rem_euclid(&-s), point3(3.0, 1.0, 0.0));
```

#### `div_euclid`

```rust
pub fn div_euclid(&self, other: &Size3D<T, U>) -> Point3D<T, U>
```

Calculates Euclidean division, the matching method for `rem_euclid`.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::point3;
use euclid::default::{Point3D, Size3D};

let p = Point3D::new(7.0, -7.0, 0.0);
let s = Size3D::new(4.0, -4.0, 12.0);

assert_eq!(p.div_euclid(&s), point3(1.0, 2.0, 0.0));
assert_eq!((-p).div_euclid(&s), point3(-2.0, -1.0, 0.0));
assert_eq!(p.div_euclid(&-s), point3(-1.0, -2.0, 0.0));
```

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::euclid::Rect`

```rust
#[repr(C)]pub struct Rect<T, U> {
    pub origin: Point2D<T, U>,
    pub size: Size2D<T, U>,
}
```

A 2d Rectangle optionally tagged with a unit.

## Representation

`Rect` is represented by an origin point and a size.

See [`Box2D`](struct.Box2D.md) for a rectangle represented by two endpoints.

## Empty rectangle

A rectangle is considered empty (see [`is_empty`](struct.Rect.md)) if any of the following is true:

- it’s area is empty,
- it’s area is negative (`size.x < 0` or `size.y < 0`),
- it contains NaNs.

Calculate the size and position of an inner rectangle.

### `impl<T, U> Rect<T, U> where T: Copy + Add<Output = T> + Sub<Output = T>,`

### `impl<T, U> Rect<T, U> where T: Copy + Zero + PartialOrd + Sub<Output = T>,`

#### `from_points`

```rust
pub fn from_points<I>(points: I) -> Rect<T, U> where I: IntoIterator, <I as IntoIterator>::Item: Borrow<Point2D<T, U>>,
```

Returns the smallest rectangle defined by the top/bottom/left/right-most points provided as parameter.

Note: This function has a behavior that can be surprising because the right-most and bottom-most points are exactly on the edge of the rectangle while the [`Rect::contains`](struct.Rect.md) function is has exclusive semantic on these edges. This means that the right-most and bottom-most points provided to [`Rect::from_points`](struct.Rect.md) will count as not contained by the rect. This behavior may change in the future.

See [`Box2D::from_points`](struct.Box2D.md) for more details.

```rust

```

Cast from one numeric representation to another, preserving the units.

When casting from floating point to integer coordinates, the decimals are truncated as one would expect from a simple cast, but this behavior does not always make sense geometrically. Consider using [`round`](struct.Rect.md), [`round_in`](struct.Rect.md) or [`round_out`](struct.Rect.md) before casting.

Fallible cast from one numeric representation to another, preserving the units.

When casting from floating point to integer coordinates, the decimals are truncated as one would expect from a simple cast, but this behavior does not always make sense geometrically. Consider using [`round`](struct.Rect.md), [`round_in`](struct.Rect.md) or [`round_out` before casting.

### `impl<T, U> Rect<T, U> where T: Floor + Ceil + Round + Add<Output = T> + Sub<Output = T>,`

#### `round`

```rust
pub fn round(&self) -> Rect<T, U>
```

Return a rectangle with edges rounded to integer coordinates, such that the returned rectangle has the same set of pixel centers as the original one. Edges at offset 0.5 round up. Suitable for most places where integral device coordinates are needed, but note that any translation should be applied first to avoid pixel rounding errors. Note that this is *not* rounding to nearest integer if the values are negative. They are always rounding as floor(n + 0.5).

###### Usage notes

Note, that when using with floating-point `T` types that method can significantly lose precision for large values, so if you need to call this method very often it is better to use [`Box2D`](struct.Box2D.md).

#### `round_in`

```rust
pub fn round_in(&self) -> Rect<T, U>
```

Return a rectangle with edges rounded to integer coordinates, such that the original rectangle contains the resulting rectangle.

###### Usage notes

Note, that when using with floating-point `T` types that method can significantly lose precision for large values, so if you need to call this method very often it is better to use [`Box2D`](struct.Box2D.md).

#### `round_out`

```rust
pub fn round_out(&self) -> Rect<T, U>
```

Return a rectangle with edges rounded to integer coordinates, such that the original rectangle is contained in the resulting rectangle.

###### Usage notes

Note, that when using with floating-point `T` types that method can significantly lose precision for large values, so if you need to call this method very often it is better to use [`Box2D`](struct.Box2D.md).

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::euclid::RigidTransform3D`

```rust
#[repr(C)]pub struct RigidTransform3D<T, Src, Dst> {
    pub rotation: Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst>,
    pub translation: Vector3D<T, Dst>,
}
```

A rigid transformation. All lengths are preserved under such a transformation.

Internally, this is a rotation and a translation, with the rotation applied first (i.e. `Rotation * Translation`, in row-vector notation)

This can be more efficient to use over full matrices, especially if you have to deal with the decomposed quantities often.

## Fields

### `translation: Vector3D<T, Dst>`

Convert `Rc<Trait>` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `Rc<Any>`. `Rc<Any>` can then be further `downcast` into `Rc<ConcreteType>` where `ConcreteType` implements `Trait`.

#### `as_any`

```rust
fn as_any(&self) -> &(dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&Any`’s vtable from `&Trait`’s.

#### `as_any_mut`

```rust
fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut (dyn Any + 'static)
```

Convert `&mut Trait` (where `Trait: Downcast`) to `&Any`. This is needed since Rust cannot generate `&mut Any`’s vtable from `&mut Trait`’s.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::euclid::Rotation2D`

```rust
pub struct Rotation2D<T, Src, Dst> {
    pub angle: T,
    /* private fields */
}
```

A transform that can represent rotations in 2d, represented as an angle in radians.

## Fields

### `angle: T`

Angle in radians

## Methods


Creates a rotation from an angle in radians.


Creates a rotation from an angle in radians.

Creates the identity rotation.

### `impl<T, Src, Dst> Rotation2D<T, Src, Dst> where T: Copy,`

#### `cast_unit`

```rust
pub fn cast_unit<Src2, Dst2>(&self) -> Rotation2D<T, Src2, Dst2>
```

Cast the unit, preserving the numeric value.

###### Example

```rust
enum Local {}
enum World {}

enum Local2 {}
enum World2 {}

let to_world: Rotation2D<_, Local, World> = Rotation2D::radians(42);

assert_eq!(to_world.angle, to_world.cast_unit::<Local2, World2>().angle);
```

#### `to_untyped`

```rust
pub fn to_untyped(&self) -> Rotation2D<T, UnknownUnit, UnknownUnit>
```

Drop the units, preserving only the numeric value.

###### Example

```rust
enum Local {}
enum World {}

let to_world: Rotation2D<_, Local, World> = Rotation2D::radians(42);

assert_eq!(to_world.angle, to_world.to_untyped().angle);
```

#### `from_untyped`

```rust
pub fn from_untyped( r: &Rotation2D<T, UnknownUnit, UnknownUnit>, ) -> Rotation2D<T, Src, Dst>
```

Tag a unitless value with units.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::UnknownUnit;
enum Local {}
enum World {}

let rot: Rotation2D<_, UnknownUnit, UnknownUnit> = Rotation2D::radians(42);

assert_eq!(rot.angle, Rotation2D::<_, Local, World>::from_untyped(&rot).angle);
```

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::euclid::Rotation3D`

```rust
pub struct Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst> {
    pub i: T,
    pub j: T,
    pub k: T,
    pub r: T,
    /* private fields */
}
```

A transform that can represent rotations in 3d, represented as a quaternion.

Most methods expect the quaternion to be normalized. When in doubt, use [`unit_quaternion`](struct.Rotation3D.md) instead of [`quaternion`](struct.Rotation3D.md) to create a rotation as the former will ensure that its result is normalized.

Some people use the `x, y, z, w` (or `w, x, y, z`) notations. The equivalence is as follows: `x -> i`, `y -> j`, `z -> k`, `w -> r`. The memory layout of this type corresponds to the `x, y, z, w` notation

## Fields

### `i: T`

Component multiplied by the imaginary number `i`.

### `j: T`

Component multiplied by the imaginary number `j`.

### `k: T`

Component multiplied by the imaginary number `k`.

### `r: T`

The real part.

## Methods

### `impl<T, Src, Dst> Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst>`

#### `quaternion`

```rust
pub fn quaternion(a: T, b: T, c: T, r: T) -> Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst>
```

Creates a rotation around from a quaternion representation.

The parameters are a, b, c and r compose the quaternion `a*i + b*j + c*k + r` where `a`, `b` and `c` describe the vector part and the last parameter `r` is the real part.

The resulting quaternion is not necessarily normalized. See [`unit_quaternion`](struct.Rotation3D.md).

#### `identity`

```rust
pub fn identity() -> Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst> where T: Zero + One,
```

Creates the identity rotation.

### `impl<T, Src, Dst> Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst> where T: Copy,`

#### `vector_part`

```rust
pub fn vector_part(&self) -> Vector3D<T, UnknownUnit>
```

Returns the vector part (i, j, k) of this quaternion.

The vector part represents the axis of the rotation.

#### `cast_unit`

```rust
pub fn cast_unit<Src2, Dst2>(&self) -> Rotation3D<T, Src2, Dst2>
```

Cast the unit, preserving the numeric value.

###### Example

```rust
enum Local {}
enum World {}

enum Local2 {}
enum World2 {}

let to_world: Rotation3D<_, Local, World> = Rotation3D::quaternion(1, 2, 3, 4);

assert_eq!(to_world.i, to_world.cast_unit::<Local2, World2>().i);
assert_eq!(to_world.j, to_world.cast_unit::<Local2, World2>().j);
assert_eq!(to_world.k, to_world.cast_unit::<Local2, World2>().k);
assert_eq!(to_world.r, to_world.cast_unit::<Local2, World2>().r);
```

#### `to_untyped`

```rust
pub fn to_untyped(&self) -> Rotation3D<T, UnknownUnit, UnknownUnit>
```

Drop the units, preserving only the numeric value.

###### Example

```rust
enum Local {}
enum World {}

let to_world: Rotation3D<_, Local, World> = Rotation3D::quaternion(1, 2, 3, 4);

assert_eq!(to_world.i, to_world.to_untyped().i);
assert_eq!(to_world.j, to_world.to_untyped().j);
assert_eq!(to_world.k, to_world.to_untyped().k);
assert_eq!(to_world.r, to_world.to_untyped().r);
```

#### `from_untyped`

```rust
pub fn from_untyped( r: &Rotation3D<T, UnknownUnit, UnknownUnit>, ) -> Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst>
```

Tag a unitless value with units.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::UnknownUnit;
enum Local {}
enum World {}

let rot: Rotation3D<_, UnknownUnit, UnknownUnit> = Rotation3D::quaternion(1, 2, 3, 4);

assert_eq!(rot.i, Rotation3D::<_, Local, World>::from_untyped(&rot).i);
assert_eq!(rot.j, Rotation3D::<_, Local, World>::from_untyped(&rot).j);
assert_eq!(rot.k, Rotation3D::<_, Local, World>::from_untyped(&rot).k);
assert_eq!(rot.r, Rotation3D::<_, Local, World>::from_untyped(&rot).r);
```

### `impl<T, Src, Dst> Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst> where T: Real,`

```rust
pub fn unit_quaternion(i: T, j: T, k: T, r: T) -> Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst>
```

Creates a rotation around from a quaternion representation and normalizes it.

The parameters are a, b, c and r compose the quaternion `a*i + b*j + c*k + r` before normalization, where `a`, `b` and `c` describe the vector part and the last parameter `r` is the real part.

#### `euler`

```rust
pub fn euler( roll: Angle<T>, pitch: Angle<T>, yaw: Angle<T>, ) -> Rotation3D<T, Src, Dst>
```

Creates a rotation from Euler angles.

The rotations are applied in roll then pitch then yaw order.

- Roll (also called bank) is a rotation around the x axis.
- Pitch (also called bearing) is a rotation around the y axis.
- Yaw (also called heading) is a rotation around the z axis.

# `iced_renderer::geometry::path::lyon_path::geom::euclid::Scale`

```rust
pub struct Scale<T, Src, Dst>(pub T, _);
```

A scaling factor between two different units of measurement.

This is effectively a type-safe float, intended to be used in combination with other types like `length::Length` to enforce conversion between systems of measurement at compile time.

`Src` and `Dst` represent the units before and after multiplying a value by a `Scale`. They may be types without values, such as empty enums. For example:

```rust
use euclid::Scale;
use euclid::Length;
enum Mm {};
enum Inch {};

let mm_per_inch: Scale<f32, Inch, Mm> = Scale::new(25.4);

let one_foot: Length<f32, Inch> = Length::new(12.0);
let one_foot_in_mm: Length<f32, Mm> = one_foot * mm_per_inch;
```

#### `is_identity`

```rust
pub fn is_identity(self) -> bool where T: PartialEq + One,
```

Returns `true` if this scale has no effect.

###### Example

```rust
use euclid::Scale;
use euclid::num::One;
enum Mm {};
enum Cm {};

let cm_per_mm: Scale<f32, Mm, Cm> = Scale::new(0.1);
let mm_per_mm: Scale<f32, Mm, Mm> = Scale::new(1.0);

assert_eq!(cm_per_mm.is_identity(), false);
assert_eq!(mm_per_mm.is_identity(), true);
assert_eq!(mm_per_mm, Scale::one());
```
